1.sense: The surah opens by swearing on the sky, and not on the sky as empty space but on the fixed formations set into it. Burj in ordinary Arabic is a tower or a fortified station, so the first thing the listener is told to look at is a height that has been built and garrisoned.

notes.t: What al-buruj names here is read more than one way. The great stars and constellations, the mansions the sun and moon pass through, and the guarded gates of the sky have all been held. The word itself is the word for a fortress tower, and every reading keeps that.
notes.src: at-Tabari records the constellations, the stations and the gates without settling on one

notes.t: An oath sworn on the sky as a structure sets the frame for what follows. The surah is about a hole dug in the ground and what was done inside it, and it begins by naming the thing above that ground.
The Qur'an uses the same word for the sky in two other places, both times in the context of what has been placed there deliberately.

links.why: We placed constellations in the sky and made it pleasing to those who look
the same word again, joined to a lamp and a shining moon

2.sense: The second oath is on a day that has not happened yet, and it is identified by nothing except the fact that it was promised. Its whole guarantee is that somebody said it would come.

notes.t: Mawʿud is a passive participle: the Day that was promised, not the Day that promises. It is fixed by an act of speech already completed, which is how an oath can be sworn on something still in the future.
The exegetes are effectively agreed that the promised Day is the Day of Resurrection, and the surah confirms it by spending the rest of its length on what is settled then.
The Qur'an makes the keeping of the promise a matter of Allah's own description rather than of circumstance.

links.why: a Day for which mankind will be gathered and which will be witnessed
the Hour is coming, and the reason it is kept hidden

3.sense: The third oath is on a witness and on the thing witnessed, and both are left indefinite. The surah is about to describe people who sat and watched, so the oath lands on the act of watching before any watcher has been named.

notes.t: This is one of the most contested pairs in the Qur'an. Friday and the Day of Arafah, the Prophet ﷺ and his community, the angels and the deeds they record, and every witness together with everything witnessed have all been argued for by serious exegetes.
notes.src: at-Tabari lists a long series of positions and prefers the general reading

notes.t: Both words are indefinite in the Arabic, which keeps them open rather than pointing at one appointed thing. The general reading is also the one that fits what the surah does four verses later, when it calls a crowd on the rim of a trench witnesses.
The root sh-h-d runs through this surah three times in nine verses: here, of the killers, and finally of Allah. The oath is planting the word it will use against them.

links.why: the same root turned on the men sitting at the fire
what it will be like when a witness is brought from every nation

4.sense: The verdict is delivered before the story. The people who dug the trench are condemned in the first words spoken about them, so what follows is not an inquiry with an open ending but the reading of an already settled charge.

notes.t: Qutila is literally killed, used in Arabic as a curse formula the way a speaker might say may he be finished. The Qur'an uses it in the same way of the falsifiers and of ungrateful man.
Ukhdud is a long cut in the ground, from the root khadd, which also gives the word for a cheek. The picture is a furrow, something dug the length of a field rather than a pit.

The Qur'an gives these people no place, no date and no names. Many exegetes attach the account to Najran in southern Arabia and to the long report of the boy, the king, the monk and the sorcerer, which ends with believers thrown into a fire. That identification comes from the historians, not from these verses.
notes.src: the long report is in Muslim 3005 and names no location; the Najran attribution is the work of later historians

links.why: the same curse formula used of those who guess at the truth
destroyed is man, how ungrateful he is

5.sense: The trench is named a second time, now by what filled it. Fuel has to be cut, carried and fed in, so the description turns the killing into a supplied project rather than a flare of temper.

notes.t: Waqud is the material burned, not the flame that comes off it. Naming the fuel names the labour: somebody gathered the wood and somebody kept feeding it while the seats were occupied.
The construction dhat, possessed of, is the same one used of the sky in verse one. Both the sky and the trench are introduced by what they hold, and the surah is about to weigh one against the other.
The Qur'an uses the fuel image for the Fire of the next life, and there the fuel is people and stones rather than wood.

links.why: the Fire whose fuel is men and stones
the kindled fire of Allah, described by its burning rather than its size

6.sense: The detail the surah picks out is the sitting. They were not fighting, not fleeing, not carrying out an order in a hurry. They had taken seats around the edge, which is what a person does when he expects to be somewhere for a while.

notes.t: Quʿud is the plural of an active participle, not a past tense verb. Arabic uses that form for a state held rather than an act completed, so the men are left sitting inside the sentence.
The preposition ʿalayha, over it, puts them on the rim looking down into the trench. The verse spends its words on posture and vantage point and says nothing at all about the people in the fire.
The seating is what makes this a scene rather than an atrocity report. A crowd that sits has decided to be an audience, and the next verse names it as one.

links.why: on that Day it is the believers on the couches, looking on
the verse that tells you what they were doing while they sat

7.sense: The word from the third oath comes back and is fastened onto them. They are witnesses, and the thing they witness is their own act, so the case against them is built out of the fact that they were present and watching.

notes.t: Shuhud answers shahid in verse three. The oath was sworn on a witness, and six verses later the surah has produced the ugliest kind of witness there is: one who watches a thing he is himself doing.
The verb yafʿalun is present tense inside a past frame. In Arabic that keeps the action running in front of the listener instead of closing it off as finished.
The victims are named only by their faith, al-mu'minin. No tribe, no age, no number. The surah gives them the single description that the next verse turns into the whole indictment.

links.why: the oath this verse cashes in
the Day their own tongues and hands and feet give evidence against them

8.sense: The charge sheet is one line long. Nothing was stolen, nothing was broken, nobody was harmed. The offence was belief. Then the verse names the One believed in with two attributes that answer the situation exactly: He is not weak, and He is worth what it cost.

notes.t: Naqama is to find fault with something and hold it against a person. The Arabic frame they held nothing against them except that is a standard way of showing that the stated grievance is no grievance at all.

The same construction is put in the mouths of Pharaoh's magicians after they believed, and again in a challenge to the People of the Book. In all three places the accusation collapses as soon as it is stated in full.

Al-Aziz is the one nothing overpowers and al-Hamid is the one who deserves praise. Placed at the end of this verse they say that the killers were not stronger than the object of that belief, only quicker.

links.why: you take revenge on us only because we believed in the signs of our Lord
do you resent us for nothing but that we believed in Allah

9.sense: The description of the One they believed in continues, and it closes on the same root a third time. The men on the rim thought they were the only witnesses in the place, and that whatever they agreed among themselves afterwards would be the record.

notes.t: Shahid is the third appearance of sh-h-d in nine verses: an unnamed witness in the oath, the killers as witnesses of their own act, and now Allah as witness over all of it. The surah has been assembling this word from the start.
A king ordered that trench dug and held a stretch of one province. The verse answers by naming what the other party owns, and the two quantities are not on the same scale.
The Qur'an states elsewhere that no deed is done except with Allah present as witness to it, and it says this to the Prophet ﷺ about his own affairs first.

links.why: you do not do a deed without Us being witnesses over you while you are in it
no private conversation of three without Him as the fourth

10.sense: The sentence widens from one trench to a standing rule. Anyone who burns believers and does not turn back afterwards receives two named punishments. The clause about repentance is left sitting in the middle of the threat, where it cannot be missed.

notes.t: Fatana is originally to put metal into fire to see what it is made of. The word carries persecution and testing in one movement, which is exactly what the trench was: a fire that asked a question.

Al-Hasan al-Basri is quoted on this verse saying to look at the generosity in it: they burned His friends alive and He is still calling them to repent. It is a scholar's remark on the wording, and the wording is the text's.
notes.src: quoted from al-Hasan al-Basri by Ibn Kathir in his commentary on this verse

notes.t: Believing men and believing women are listed separately rather than under one plural. The verse counts the victims in both columns instead of letting the masculine plural cover them.

links.why: do not despair of the mercy of Allah, said to those who went furthest
repentance that turns the record itself over

11.sense: Against a trench of fire, gardens with water running underneath them. The pairing is deliberate and so is the last word. This is called the great winning, and it is said about people who were burned alive in front of a seated crowd and who by every visible measure lost.

notes.t: Fawz is the word for coming out of a contest safe and ahead. Applied here it reverses the verdict of the day itself, when the men with the fuel walked home and the believers did not.
The usual Qur'anic pairing is al-fawz al-ʿazim, the immense attainment. Here it is al-fawz al-kabir, the great one, and the phrase in this exact form occurs only in this place.
The Qur'an ties the same gardens to the same two conditions, faith and righteous work, in dozens of places, and calls the result an attainment there too.

links.why: the same gardens and the same word for winning
whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to the Garden has won

12.sense: The surah turns and speaks to one person for the first time, and what it says to him is about grip. Batsh is not a sentence handed down from a distance. It is a hand closing on something.

notes.t: Batsh is a violent seizing, the word for grabbing a man by force. Arabic has quieter words for punishment and the verse does not use them.

Your Lord, said to the Prophet ﷺ, places this sentence in the middle of a small and pressed community rather than in the mouth of a state. The consolation is that the grip belongs to the side that currently has none.
The same root names the day of the greatest seizing, where it is given as the direct answer to a people who thought the matter was closed.

links.why: the Day We seize with the greatest seizure
the grip of your Lord on a town that wronged, said with a different verb

13.sense: The grip in the verse before is backed here by two verbs. A power that could only destroy would have no answer to a trench full of dead believers. One that starts a thing and returns it does.

notes.t: Both verbs are given without an object, which leaves them general. He begins and He brings back, and the sentence does not restrict what the thing is.
Yuʿid is the standard Qur'anic term for the second creation, and the Qur'an argues from it: bringing a thing back is the easier of the two by any reckoning a human being has.
Placed between the severe seizing of verse twelve and the forgiveness of verse fourteen, this verse is the hinge. Restoration is what makes both the threat and the pardon mean anything.

links.why: He begins creation then repeats it, and that is easier for Him
the return of all of you together, stated as a promise in truth

14.sense: Two verses after the severe grip, two names of pardon and warmth. Wadud is built on wudd, the ordinary affection that passes between people, and it is not a distant word.

notes.t: Al-Wadud occurs twice in the whole Qur'an. Here, and on the lips of Shuʿayb telling his people that his Lord is Merciful and Loving while they are threatening to stone him.
Whether wadud means the One who loves or the One who is loved is discussed by the grammarians, since the pattern faʿul can carry either. Most carry the active sense, and some hold both at once.
notes.src: at-Tabari carries He loves His obedient servants; others read it as the One His servants love

notes.t: The placement is the argument. The names of pardon are given to the same audience that was just told about the seizing, and in the same breath as the promise that He brings things back.

links.why: the only other place the name al-Wadud appears
affection appointed for those who believe and work righteousness

15.sense: A throne is named, and the surah has already shown a man on one. A king ordered a furrow dug and sat above it. The One described here owns the Throne and everything the Throne stands over.

notes.t: The canonical readings differ on the last vowel. With damma, al-Majidu describes the Owner; with kasra, al-Majidi describes the Throne. Both are transmitted and both are recited. The reading in this Mushaf has the damma.
notes.src: the ten readings split on the final vowel; Hafs from Asim reads al-Majīdu

notes.t: Majd in Arabic joins two things English separates: greatness of standing, and generosity with what that standing allows. A majid is not merely exalted, he gives.
The Qur'an attaches the Throne to Allah repeatedly and always with an adjective of scale, which keeps the word from being read as a seat.

links.why: Lord of the mighty Throne, given as what to say when people turn away
the Throne named noble at the close of an argument about creation

16.sense: The word is in the intensive pattern, so it is not one who does but one who does and keeps doing. Nothing stands between the intention and the event, which is the answer to a story in which men with fuel and seats appeared to have the last word.

notes.t: Faʿʿal is the Arabic shape for a settled occupation. It is the pattern behind khabbaz for a baker and najjar for a carpenter: not one who once baked, but the one whose work this is.
The same phrase closes a passage in Surah Hud, where it is said about the fate of two groups after the Day, and there too it comes at the end of a stretch about outcomes nobody can appeal.

Three verses have now described Allah by what He does rather than by what He is like: He begins and brings back, He forgives and loves, He carries out what He intends. The surah is answering an audience that had watched action and been impressed by it.

links.why: the identical phrase, closing a passage on the two destinations
His command when He intends a thing

17.sense: A question is put to the listener, and it already assumes the answer. The surah turns from a trench nobody could locate to two names every Arab could recite from memory.

notes.t: Hal ataka is a Qur'anic opening formula for a story the audience half knows. It is used the same way at the head of Surah Al-Ghashiya and before the account of Musa in the valley.
Junud means armies, and it is the word chosen instead of kings, peoples or nations. It names the thing about them that mattered to onlookers, which is the thing about to be shown as no protection.
Hadith here means an account or a report. The Qur'an uses the ordinary word for news to introduce two of the most catastrophic endings in its history sections.

links.why: the same question used to open a surah about the Day
has the account of Musa come to you, put to the same listener

18.sense: Two names and nothing else. One ran the largest state in its region and the other cut houses out of solid rock. Neither story is retold, because the audience already had both and the point is the ending, not the plot.

notes.t: Pharaoh went down in water and Thamud were taken by a cry and a shaking of the ground. Two different sorts of strength, two different instruments, one result each.
The Qur'an pairs these two elsewhere as the standard examples of a people who could not be argued with and were removed anyway. In Surah Al-Fajr they are named in consecutive verses.
Thamud is told at length in the surah that sits six places after this one, which is why the two reward being read together: this verse gives the name, Ash-Shams gives the day it ended.

links.why: the full Thamud account, from the denial to the levelling
the same two named side by side, with the rock cutting specified

19.sense: The examples did not land. The verse does not say the deniers hold an opinion or made an argument. It says they are inside denial, the way a person is inside a room, which describes a location rather than a conclusion.

notes.t: Bal is the particle of correction. It cancels the expectation raised by the question two verses earlier: yes, the account reached them, and no, it changed nothing.
Fi takdhib uses the preposition of containment. Arabic could have said they deny, and instead the verse makes denial the space they occupy and leaves them standing in it.
The Qur'an distinguishes elsewhere between not knowing and rejecting what one has recognised, and it puts the deniers of the Prophet ﷺ in the second category by name.

links.why: they do not call you a liar, they reject the signs of Allah knowingly
they denied while their own selves were convinced

20.sense: They are inside denial and He is around the outside of it. Wara' means behind and it also means beyond, and either way the picture is of a wall at their back that they have not turned round to see.

notes.t: Muhit is the participle of a verb meaning to surround on every side. The same root gives al-muhit, the name Arabic uses for the ocean that goes all the way round.
This answers verse six precisely. Men sat around a trench and believed they had it surrounded, and the surah closes the geometry by putting somebody around them.
The Qur'an states the encompassing directly and without a metaphor at the end of Surah Fussilat, where it is offered as the last word of a long argument about signs.

links.why: He encompasses all things, given as the closing statement of an argument
the men who thought they were the ones doing the surrounding

21.sense: The second correction in three verses. Whatever they have decided to call this, it is a recitation that carries glory, and the word used for it is the same word used six verses earlier for the Owner of the Throne.

notes.t: Majid ties the Book to the Throne by vocabulary. The surah has spent its second half naming what cannot be reached by men with fuel, and it ends the list with the recitation itself.
Qur'an means a reading aloud, from qara'a. The Book names itself by the act of being recited rather than by being written down, which is what the last verse then has to correct.
Other surahs swear by this Book with an adjective attached, and the choice of adjective changes with the argument being made.

links.why: an oath sworn by the glorious Qur'an at the head of a surah about resurrection
the recitation described as noble in the middle of a similar denial

22.sense: The last words of the surah put the recitation somewhere out of reach. Men with wood and a trench could burn bodies in an afternoon and could not touch this, which is the whole distance the surah has been measuring.

notes.t: The canonical readings differ on the last vowel. In the genitive it is the tablet that is guarded; in the nominative it is the Qur'an that is guarded, wherever the tablet may be. This Mushaf reads the genitive.
notes.src: the ten readings split on the final vowel of maḥfūẓ; Hafs from Asim reads the genitive

notes.t: Lawh is an ordinary word for a board or plank. The Qur'an uses the plural of it for the timbers of Nuh's ship, which keeps the image from floating away into abstraction.
The surah opened with a sky held in position by towers and closes with a Book held in position on a tablet. Both ends are about something fixed above a world where nothing was.

links.why: We sent down the Reminder and We are its guardian
in a Book kept concealed, said of the same recitation
